# Resilience review

Examine each remote call, queue, and shared resource in the change.

| Item | Good practice | Common defect |
|---|---|---|
| Timeout | Each remote call has a connect and a read timeout, smaller than the timeout of the caller. | No timeout, or the default of the library (often infinite). |
| Retries | Only for idempotent operations and transient errors. Exponential backoff, jitter, and a maximum. One layer retries, not each layer. | Retry storms: each layer retries, so one failure multiplies the load. |
| Idempotency | Writes that can repeat (retries, redelivery) use an idempotency key or a natural key. | A retried payment or order runs two times. |
| Circuit breaker | Opens on a high error rate or slow calls. Has a fallback or a fast failure. Shares state when the service has many instances, if the project needs it. | The breaker opens, but the caller has no fallback and fails slowly anyway. |
| Bulkhead | Separate pools or limits for each dependency, so that one slow dependency does not block all threads. | One shared pool for all remote calls. |
| Load shedding | The service rejects work early (429 or 503) when it is full. Queues have a maximum size. | Unbounded queues and memory growth until the process dies. |
| Graceful degradation | A non-critical feature can fail without failing the request (a cached value, a default, or no recommendation). | A failure of an optional dependency fails the main journey. |
| Backpressure | Consumers control the rate. Producers react to slow consumers. | Fast producers fill the broker or the memory. |
| Capacity | The expected load, the resource use for each request, and the limits are written with numbers. | "It should be fine." |
| Startup and shutdown | Readiness waits for the dependencies that are necessary. Shutdown drains the requests in progress. | Traffic arrives before the service is ready, or requests fail during each deploy. |

## Output

For each item, write PASS, FAIL, or NOT APPLICABLE, with the file and the line. For each FAIL, give the risk and the fix. Propose a check when a command or a test can prove the behavior, for example a test where the dependency times out and the service returns the fallback.
